exit_trigger: Moat erosion: the franchise test fails, meaning ROE is at or above 15% in fewer than 80% of reported fiscal years; Management failure: negative reported annual operating cash flow, or evidence of dishonesty or value-destroying acquisitions; Extreme overvaluation: price persistently above 1.5x the owner-earnings intrinsic value; Evidence that technology is permanently eroding pricing power or client retention
rationale: I own three shares of Accenture, bought three days ago at $251.845, and they are now $222.70, down 11.57%. Three days of price tells me nothing about the business, so I'm not going to trade on it. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 26.9% and a debt-to-equity of 0.32. Owner earnings averaged about $9.26 billion against a market cap of about $134 billion, and the model puts value near $437 per share, a 50% margin of safety. That model uses a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, so I'd haircut it. My real worry is whether a people-based services moat holds up against fast technological change, and I can't settle that from this snapshot. I keep the position, I don't add until I've checked the evidence the snapshot lacks, and I don't sell just because Mr. Market is in a mood.

exit_trigger: Not applicable: no position. I would revisit only if I could name a durable moat and judge its ten-year economics with confidence.
rationale: I don't own this one, and I'm not going to start. The numbers in front of me look good: a 5-year average ROE of 22.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.43, a market cap of about $6.9 billion, and a price well under the computed intrinsic value of $75.94 a share. But a cheap price on a business I can't confidently handicap ten years out is exactly the trap Charlie and I try to avoid. As I understand it, this is a labor-intensive business-process and IT services outfit. I can't say what AI and automation will do to its economics over the next decade, and I don't see a moat I can name with confidence. A moat that has to be rebuilt every year is no moat at all, so I'll pass and wait for a pitch right in my sweet spot.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE below 15% in more than 20% of up to ten fiscal years; Negative annual operating cash flow reported in the newest five fiscal years; Evidence the brand is discounting heavily or losing pricing power to competitors; Price exceeds 1.5x intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or is found to be dishonest
rationale: We own ten shares, bought at $128.38 and now marked at $110.05, down 14.28% in 104 days. A price drop alone is never a reason to sell, so the question is whether the brand still earns its keep. The numbers say it does: a five-year average ROE of 34.6%, debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, and five-year average owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a market cap of about $11.6 billion. I would not lean on the model's $363 intrinsic value, because it assumes 8% growth discounted at 5% and a small change in those inputs moves it a lot. What I cannot verify from this snapshot is ten years of positive earnings, CEO tenure, or insider activity, and apparel is fashion-driven, which is exactly where moats must be rebuilt every season. So I keep what we own and add nothing until I can see that the brand still commands full prices.

exit_trigger: Evidence that generative-AI competitors are eroding Adobe's pricing power or subscriber retention; Return on equity falling below 15% on a sustained basis; Negative operating cash flow or management capital-allocation failures; Price rising above 1.5x the owner-earnings intrinsic value
rationale: I do not own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are attractive: a 5-year average ROE of about 40%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price well under the owner-earnings value of $467.50 per share that the snapshot reports. But a cheap-looking price is not a thesis. The snapshot says nothing about ten years of earnings, management tenure, or customer retention, and I cannot check those from here. The business is also exposed to rapid technological change, because generative AI could erode the switching costs that protect the creative-software franchise, and I have been wary of moats that must be rebuilt every few years. The 8% growth and 5% discount rate behind that value are generous inputs. I will wait until I can verify the earnings record and convince myself the moat survives the next decade, and until then I stay on the sidelines.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of the up-to-ten fiscal years measured; Management failure: a reported negative annual operating cash flow in any of the newest five fiscal years, or evidence of dishonesty or value-destroying acquisitions; Extreme overvaluation: price above 1.5x the owner-earnings intrinsic value (about $390 a share on today's $260.01 estimate); Structural erosion of the dealer-franchise model, such as manufacturers' direct sales weakening dealer economics
rationale: I own this one, and the question is whether to keep it. It is a car and truck dealer, a business I can explain, though not one with a fortress moat. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.8% and debt-to-equity of 0.40, and my conservative owner-earnings value of $260.01 a share against a $212.41 price gives an 18.3% margin of safety. That value assumes zero growth, which I like, but I could not check ten years of earnings, CEO tenure or ROIC from what I was given, so I will not add. I'm down about 2% since August, and a lower price alone has never been a reason to sell. I keep the shares and wait for the missing evidence.

exit_trigger: Moat erosion: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years, i.e. the franchise test fails; Management failure: negative annual operating cash flow reported, or evidence of dishonesty or value-destroying acquisitions; Extreme overvaluation: price persistently above 1.5x intrinsic value; Loss of sole-source status on major submarine or vehicle programs, or a structural shift in defense procurement that undermines pricing
rationale: We own this one, and I'm content to keep it. General Dynamics builds submarines, combat vehicles and business jets, and much of that work is sole-source and sits behind security clearances and decades of government relationships, which is a moat I can understand. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.32, which is the kind of return on equity without leverage I like. At $348.87 against an owner-earnings DCF value of $417.18, the margin of safety is 16.4%, only a hair above my 15% bar, so I would add only on a better price. I'm also uneasy that the value leans on an 8% growth assumption and that owner earnings are only about 4.1% of market cap, which is thin. We're down 1.2% after 22 days, and a price wobble that size is no reason to act.

exit_trigger: ROE falls below 15% in a sustained way, showing moat erosion; Negative operating cash flow or evidence of management dishonesty or poor capital allocation; Price persistently above 1.5x intrinsic value; Loss of pricing power or share to e-commerce or larger distributors
rationale: I own 11 shares of MSM, bought at $120.05 and now marked at $109.535, a loss of 8.76% in 24 days. A price decline of that size is not a reason to sell if the business is intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 19.4% and debt-to-equity of 0.33, and an owner-earnings DCF value of about $129.83 a share against $109.54, a 15.6% margin of safety. That is just above my 15% threshold, so I keep the position but would not chase it. The moat here is switching costs and service convenience in industrial distribution. It is real but modest, and the snapshot gives me no evidence on pricing power or customer retention, so I hold rather than add aggressively.

exit_trigger: 5-year ROE falls below 15% in a sustained way, which would show moat erosion; Negative annual operating cash flow signaling management or business failure; Price above 1.5x owner-earnings intrinsic value on a persistent basis; Evidence that heat pump or tankless shifts permanently erode the brand's pricing power
rationale: I own A. O. Smith, and I'm content to keep owning it. It makes water heaters and treatment products, a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of about 23.7% with debt-to-equity of 0.37, which is the kind of return on equity without leverage I like. The owner-earnings DCF gives roughly $98.59 a share against a price of $63.35, a 36% margin of safety, though that rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat the figure with some humility. We're up only about 3% over 27 days, which tells me nothing either way. I can't verify from this snapshot the ten-year earnings record, the CEO's tenure, or the insider activity, so my confidence is moderate, not high. No sell trigger is met, and the price is far below intrinsic value, so we keep the shares and let time work.
